sources.news_title: US President Donald Trump says US hitting Iran 'very hard’
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump says US hitting Iran 'very hard’
US President Donald Trump said that the latest US strikes on Iran were being carried out in honour of US service members killed in recent days, the Guardian reported on Monday.
“We hit them very hard again tonight, and we did that in honour of the probably three, it’s probably three great patriots,” said Trump.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency stated early Monday that a vessel was on fire off the coast of Oman. The statement said, "UKMTO has received a report of an incident 8NM northwest of Kumzar, Oman. UKMTO has received information from a verified source that a vessel is on fire.”
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that two oil tankers were blown up after attempting to transit the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian military stated that the critical waterway will not be safe for petrochemical products or 'single drop of oil and gas' transit as long as US actions in the region continue. The IRGC added that it targeted US aircraft at Jordan's aqaba airport with ballistic missiles.
Early Monday, Iranian media reported on US attacks on the Iranian city of Tabriz. Multiple explosions were also reported in southwestern Bandar Mahshahr and Bandar Imam Khomeini. Mehr news agency said there are several explosions heard in southeastern Chabahar.
Market reaction
Crude oil prices attract some buyers following these headlines. At the time of writing, the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is up 2.12% on the day at $83.50.
WTI Oil FAQs
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.
Author
Lallalit Srijandorn
FXStreet
Lallalit Srijandorn is a Parisian at heart. She has lived in France since 2019 and now becomes a digital entrepreneur based in Paris and Bangkok.

sources.news_title: New U.S. Strikes on Iran Deepen Human and Economic Toll
sources.text:
New U.S. Strikes on Iran Deepen Human and Economic Toll
Another American service member has died as military attacks widen, household costs rise and voters, especially younger Americans, question whether the war serves the nation.
The U.S. strikes on Iran entered a ninth consecutive night early Monday local time after the military announced another American service member had died. At least 17 U.S. service members have now been killed and more than 430 wounded since the war began on February 28, according to military statements and news reports. Beyond the battlefield, the conflict is also reaching American families through higher fuel costs, economic uncertainty and growing doubts about a war most voters did not support.
The latest U.S. attacks targeted Iranian bridges, electrical facilities and sites associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. U.S. Central Command said the strikes were intended to reduce Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping and civilian crews in the Strait of Hormuz.
But the expanding target list raises a difficult question: Can Washington weaken Iran’s military without causing greater harm to civilians, American troops and the global economy?
Another U.S. Service Member Killed in Iraq
The latest American death occurred Saturday during what the military described as the “controlled detonation” of a downed Iranian drone in Iraq. Another service member was reportedly injured during the operation.
The death came shortly after an Iranian attack on an airbase in Jordan killed two American service members. Four others required hospitalization, and one service member was listed as missing. The military later said “unidentified remains” were recovered Sunday and were being examined.
As of early Monday local time:
- 17 U.S. service members had been killed since the war began.
- More than 430 American personnel had been wounded.
- One set of unidentified remains recovered in Jordan had not yet been publicly identified.
- Additional injuries may be reported as military assessments continue.
Those figures represent more than statistics. Each casualty affects a family, a military unit and a community that must live with the consequences long after the headlines move on.
President Donald Trump said the latest strikes were carried out in honor of the fallen service members.
“We hit them very hard again tonight,” Trump said, according to The Associated Press.
Supporters of the military response argue that Iran cannot be allowed to attack American troops without consequences. They say force is needed to protect U.S. personnel, preserve freedom of navigation and prevent Tehran from controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
Critics respond that every new strike creates another opportunity for retaliation, placing more American troops in danger.
U.S. Strikes Expand to Bridges and Electrical Facilities
Central Command announced the latest round of attacks as part of an operation targeting Iranian military capabilities connected to attacks on shipping.
“The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” Central Command said.
The renewed campaign has included attacks on Revolutionary Guard facilities, missile positions, bridges and electrical infrastructure.
International humanitarian law generally protects civilian infrastructure, including power plants and bridges. Those protections can be reduced when a site is used for military purposes. Even then, an attack must be proportionate and designed to limit civilian harm.
That distinction is becoming increasingly important. Electricity, transportation and water systems serve ordinary families even when governments claim they also support military operations.
Iran also said a U.S. strike hit the construction site of a planned nuclear power plant in southwestern Iran. The International Atomic Energy Agency said the site was in the very early stages of construction and contained no nuclear material when inspectors last visited.
Iran Retaliates Across the Gulf
Iran has responded by launching missiles and drones toward U.S.-allied countries across the Middle East.
Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait activated air defenses during the latest attacks. Jordan’s military said it intercepted several Iranian missiles and reported no casualties or damage in that particular incident.
Missiles launched toward the Jordanian port city of Aqaba also raised concerns in neighboring Israel. Israeli officials warned that missiles or falling debris could cross into Israeli territory and trigger another round of direct fighting.
The danger is no longer limited to Iran and the United States. Nearly every Gulf Arab state has faced attacks, warnings or disruptions connected to the conflict.
Kuwait’s Water System Comes Under Attack
Kuwait reported that one of its power and water desalination plants was attacked for the second time in two days. Fires were reported, although Kuwaiti officials said the country’s power grid remained stable.
The attack is especially serious because approximately 90 percent of Kuwait’s drinking water comes from desalination. Damage to those facilities could threaten civilians who have no role in military decisions.
Jasem Mohamed al-Budaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council, accused Iran of committing war crimes by striking civilian facilities and essential infrastructure.
Iranian authorities, meanwhile, said at least 50 people were killed and 517 wounded in the latest U.S. strikes. Those figures could not be independently verified in full, but they illustrate the widening human toll claimed by both sides.
What the Iran War Is Costing Average Americans
For most Americans, the war may feel distant until its effects appear at the gas pump, grocery store or family budget.
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy routes. Before the war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through the waterway. Shipping traffic has since slowed sharply, while attacks, blockades and threats have increased the risks faced by tankers and commercial crews.
Benchmark Brent crude climbed above $90 a barrel Monday, adding pressure to an energy market already disrupted by the fighting.
Higher oil prices can affect Americans in several ways:
- Gasoline becomes more expensive. Crude oil is a major part of the cost of fuel.
- Transportation costs increase. Trucking, aviation and shipping companies pay more for fuel.
- Food and consumer prices may rise. Businesses often pass at least part of their added costs to customers.
- Household budgets become tighter. Lower-income and working-class families spend a larger share of their income on transportation and basic needs.
- Economic uncertainty grows. Businesses may delay hiring or investment when energy prices and supply routes become less predictable.
A March Ipsos poll found that 87 percent of Americans expected gas prices to continue rising. A majority said higher fuel prices were already affecting their household finances. Another Ipsos survey found that 53 percent expected the conflict to have a negative effect on their personal finances.
For families already struggling with rent, food, insurance and utility bills, another energy price shock is not an abstract foreign-policy matter. It can mean fewer groceries, delayed medical care or another month carrying credit-card debt.
Most Americans Want the War to End
Public opinion has remained skeptical of the conflict.
A June Quinnipiac University poll found that 60 percent of registered voters believed U.S. military action against Iran was not worth it, while 34 percent said it was worthwhile.
The same poll found:
- 62 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of Iran.
- 45 percent believed the war had left the United States weaker internationally.
- 59 percent lacked confidence that the temporary agreement with Iran would succeed.
- 48 percent believed the United States was too supportive of Israel.
“After months of diplomatic fits and starts, global economic repercussions and a broad loss of life in the region, a majority of voters make their feelings clear: the Iran war was a bad idea,” Quinnipiac polling analyst Tim Malloy said.
An Ipsos poll conducted in late March found that 66 percent of Americans wanted the United States to end its involvement quickly, even if Washington could not achieve every goal. Only 27 percent favored continuing the war until all U.S. objectives were achieved.
Younger Americans Are Especially Skeptical
Younger Americans have grown up during decades of military operations in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria and other parts of the Middle East.
Many have watched wars begin with promises of quick victories, only to become longer, more expensive and more complicated. Some have family members who served. Others entered adulthood during economic crises while the federal government continued spending heavily on overseas military operations.
A University of Maryland Critical Issues Poll conducted by Ipsos found that 55 percent of Americans under 35 believed the Iran war had affected U.S. interests more negatively than positively. Among adults 35 and older, 57 percent shared that view.
Only 11 percent of adults under 35 said the United States had won or was winning the war, compared with 18 percent of older adults.
That does not mean younger Americans are unconcerned about Iran’s government, its nuclear ambitions or attacks on U.S. forces. It means many do not see an open-ended war as the best solution.
Their concerns often center on several issues:
- The safety of American service members
- Civilian deaths and damage to essential services
- Rising gasoline and consumer prices
- The lack of clear limits on U.S. military involvement
- The possibility of another long Middle Eastern war
- Whether Congress and the public were given a meaningful voice
Opposition to the conflict also extends beyond young voters and the political left. Polling shows skepticism among independents and a segment of Republican voters who favor a more restrained foreign policy.
Supporters Say Military Pressure Is Necessary
A balanced assessment must recognize the argument for continued military action.
Iran has attacked American personnel, commercial vessels and facilities in neighboring countries. Its missiles and drones have threatened civilian populations and essential infrastructure. Supporters of the U.S. operation argue that failing to respond would invite more attacks and weaken American alliances.
They also contend that Iran’s control over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz could allow Tehran to pressure the global economy.
Those are serious concerns.
However, military force is not measured only by the targets it destroys. It must also be judged by whether it makes Americans safer, reduces threats and creates a realistic path toward peace.
So far, the casualty count is rising, attacks are spreading and oil markets remain unsettled.
The Diplomatic Window Is Narrowing, Not Yet Closed
The temporary agreement established a 60-day period for negotiations over a permanent end to the war and Iran’s nuclear program.
Contrary to some early accounts, the full 60-day negotiating window has not expired. The halfway point has passed, and the agreement is showing signs of collapse as both governments resume attacks.
Diplomacy may now be more difficult, but that makes it more necessary.
Congress should demand clear answers about:
- The military mission and its legal authority
- The conditions required to end U.S. strikes
- The strategy for protecting deployed personnel
- The expected financial cost to taxpayers
- The risk of prolonged disruption in the Strait of Hormuz
- The diplomatic plan for preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon
Americans should also ask their elected representatives where they stand. Supporting the troops must include more than honoring those who die. It must include careful decisions about when they are placed in danger.
America Needs a Clear Path Away From Wider War
The latest U.S. strikes may destroy Iranian military equipment and demonstrate that attacks on American troops carry a price. But retaliation alone is not a complete strategy.
Seventeen American service members have already been killed, and more than 430 have been wounded. Civilians across the region are losing relatives, homes, electricity and access to essential services. American families are facing higher energy costs while many voters say the war has not strengthened the country.
The United States must protect its personnel and allies. It must also avoid turning a dangerous conflict into an unlimited war without a clear goal or public mandate.
Readers can contact members of Congress, ask for public hearings on the mission and demand regular reporting on casualties, costs and diplomatic efforts. The nation owes its service members, and the public, a strategy built around security, accountability and a credible route to peace.
Source Note: This article was developed from the submitted research brief and publication requirements.

sources.news_title: ‘We hit them very hard again tonight’, Trump
sources.text:
US strikes Iran again, Iran says oil tankers exploded
Nayera Abdallah and Eman Abouhassira and Enas Alashray |
US forces have hit Iran for a ninth consecutive day as concerns grow over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran said two oil tankers had exploded and been immobilised.
In a statement, US Central Command said it had begun “a new wave of strikes” aimed at “degrading” Iran’s ability to attack commercial vessels in the strait’s vital shipping lanes.
Iran responded by launching an attack targeting Bahrain, the home of the US Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The strikes are part of an escalating cycle of attacks between the US and Iran after an interim ceasefire agreement signed a month ago unravelled, deepening a struggle for control over the Strait of Hormuz that has disrupted energy supplies and stoked fears of global inflation.
Both sides have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency said US missiles struck several Iranian cities early on Monday.
Explosions were heard in Tabriz, Chabahar, Konarak, Bandar Mahshahr and Bandar Imam Khomeini, according to Tasnim.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States would continue to target Iran while it attacked global commercial shipping.
“As long as Iran insists on controlling an international waterway, we’re gonna have to respond to that. The United States always remains open to a diplomatic solution,” Rubio said.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced a surprise strike against “the enemy’s special operations headquarters in Syria’s Al-Tanf area”.
The Revolutionary Guards also said they targeted US aircraft at Jordan’s Aqaba airport with ballistic missiles.
Iran earlier conducted a drone attack on US military assets and equipment at Kuwait’s Al-Adiri camp and Ali Al Salem Air Base, Iranian state TV reported early on Sunday.
Kuwait’s government said a desalination plant was attacked for the second day running, causing a fire, in what it called a direct strike on vital civilian infrastructure.
Concerns about the flow of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have persisted since the United States and Iran resumed open hostilities after accusing each other of repeatedly violating a ceasefire deal.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said late on Sunday that it received a report that a vessel was on fire not far from the Omani coast, although it had not verified a cause.
The Revolutionary Guards said on Monday that two oil tankers had exploded and been immobilised after attempting to transit what it described as an unsafe southern route through Hormuz, alleging the vessels had been encouraged by the US military to use the passage.
The statement gave no details on the vessels’ names, flags, crews or any casualties.
The Guards said the waterway would remain unsafe as long as what it called US “aggression” in the region continued, warning that “this passage will not be safe for the transit of petrochemical products, nor even a single drop of oil and gas”.
Four vessels made the transit through Hormuz on Sunday, down from eight the previous day, LSEG data showed.
At least three oil products’ tankers and one Very Large Crude Carrier have entered the strait since Friday to load oil, the data showed.
Oil prices rose two per cent to more than $US90 ($A129) a barrel on Monday.
In the latest American casualty reported in the war, the US military said a service member was killed on Saturday in northern Iraq, where the US has military bases, during a controlled detonation of what Central Command called unexploded ordnance on a downed Iranian attack drone.
The US military said earlier that two service personnel died in Jordan and that a third was missing in action. On Sunday, Central Command said that “unidentified remains” had been found at the site of Friday’s attack and that “an examination process to verify the remains is ongoing”.
“We hit them very hard again tonight,” US President Donald Trump said.
“And we did that in honour of the” soldiers killed, he said.
The latest casualty announcements brought the total number of US military personnel killed since the war began to 17, with more than 420 others wounded.
The conflict, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, seeking to disable Tehran’s nuclear and missile programs and weaken its regional proxies, has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon.

sources.news_title: US forces launch new wave of strikes against Iran - OrissaPOST
sources.text:
Washington: US forces launched a new round of strikes against Iran at the Commander in Chief’s direction, the US Central Command said in a statement.
“Today at 6 pm ET, U.S. forces began launching new airstrikes against Iran at the Commander in Chief’s direction,” CENTCOM posted on X.
“The strikes are designed to further degrade Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and swiftly punish Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces who launched attacks against American service members in Jordan last night,” according to the command.
Early Saturday, the command said that two US service members were killed and one remains missing after a strike on a base in Jordan Friday.
The deaths bring the total number of US military personnel killed to 16 since the United States and Israel launched attacks Iran February 28.
Earlier, US forces ended the seventh consecutive night of strikes against Iran July 17 at 9:30 pm ET.
“U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) hit surveillance sites, military logistics infrastructure, underground weapons storage, and maritime capabilities. U.S. forces employed fighter aircraft, aerial drones, and warships in addition to other assets,” according to the command.
CENTCOM continues to hold Iran accountable at the Commander in Chief’s direction while fully enforcing a naval blockade against Iranian ports, the statement said, adding, “More than 50,000 American service members are operating across the Middle East and remain vigilant, lethal, and ready.”
The United States has launched waves of strikes on military sites and infrastructure in Iran’s southern provinces in the past week, claiming they were aimed at “degrading Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping” in the Strait of Hormuz.
